summary: Find the minimum element of a rotated sorted array of distinct values in O(log n).
mainInsight: In a rotated sorted array one half around mid is always sorted. Compare nums[mid] with nums[right]: if nums[mid] > nums[right] the minimum lies in the right half (mid + 1 .. right); otherwise it lies in the left half including mid.
canonicalApproach: Binary search comparing mid with right

approaches.name: Linear scan / min()
approaches.summary: Take the minimum of the array.
weaknesses: Ignores the sorted structure; fails the O(log n) requirement

approaches.name: Binary search comparing mid with right
approaches.summary: Shrink toward the pivot using nums[mid] vs nums[right].

personalSolution.notes: Passes the judge but does not satisfy the O(log n) requirement. Learn and be ready to write the binary search.

promptVariants: How do you find the rotation pivot in O(log n)?
Which comparison decides the search direction?
cards.explanation: If nums[mid] > nums[right] the pivot (minimum) is to the right of mid; otherwise it is at mid or to its left.

incorrectOptionExplanations.Compare nums[mid] with nums[0] only: Works for some cases but is error-prone without the right-end comparison (all elements may be >= nums[0] in an unrotated array).
incorrectOptionExplanations.Hash the values: Does not find the minimum faster.

promptVariants: Why is the minimum in the right half when nums[mid] > nums[right]?
Why do we keep mid when nums[mid] <= nums[right]?
cards.answer: If nums[mid] > nums[right] the sequence must descend somewhere between mid and right (the pivot), so the minimum lies strictly right of mid. Otherwise the segment mid..right is sorted ascending, so the minimum is at mid or in the left part; mid itself could be the minimum, so keep it (right = mid).
keyPoints: mid > right => pivot to the right
cards.explanation: Distinct values avoid the ambiguous equality case.

promptVariants: Your solution is `return min(nums)`. What is its complexity and what would an interviewer expect?
cards.answer: min(nums) is O(n) time and ignores the rotation property; the problem requires O(log n). Expected: lo, hi = 0, n - 1; while lo < hi: mid = (lo + hi) // 2; if nums[mid] > nums[hi]: lo = mid + 1 else: hi = mid; return nums[lo].
keyPoints: mid > hi => lo = mid + 1 else hi = mid
cards.explanation: This is a common trap: the shortcut passes LeetCode but fails the interview.
